title: The Jackal and the Lion's Share
subtitle: Rukmini's secret message to Krishna
story:
The message had crossed half the country to reach Krishna in Dwaraka, but he asked after the messenger before he asked after the message.

He received the brahmana — the priest-messenger from Vidarbha — with honor, and with questions that showed he had thought about the man before him. Was the traveler's life still keeping to the old rules of his calling? For a brahmana, Krishna said, should be content with whatever comes to him by chance; a man who could not be satisfied, even if he were a lord of the gods, would wander from world to world and never find rest. He asked whether the brahmanas of Vidarbha were well — good men content with their own gains, friends to all beings — and he asked how the traveler had crossed the wild country that lay between their lands. The brahmana answered fittingly. Then he gave Krishna what he had carried so far: Rukmini's words, delivered as she had spoken them.

"I have heard of your virtues," her message ran, "and my heart has entered into you and is not ashamed. Your goodness, entering through the ear, takes away the body's distress, and the sight of you would be reward enough for any seeing eye. What wise girl of a good family, knowing what I know, would not choose you? You have no equal in family, in conduct, in beauty, in learning, in youth, in wealth. You are the one I have chosen. I have given myself to you. Do not let the king of Cedi touch the hero's share — do not let Shishupala, like a jackal, seize the lion's prey."

Then her words turned to what must be done, and the princess of Kundina laid out her whole heart and her whole plan in the same breath. "If the Lord whom the world worships with sacrifices, gifts, and vows — the Lord honored among gods, priests, and elders — is pleased with my devotion, let him come and take my hand. Not Damaghosha's son, Shishupala. Not any other. Tomorrow they will marry me. Come to Vidarbha in secret, your warriors around you; break the forces of the king of Cedi and the king of Magadha; and carry me off by the rakshasa rite — the old rite in which a bride is taken by force — as the prize of your valour. But how could you take me while I live within the inner apartments, without striking down my own kinsmen? I will show you the way. The day before the wedding there is a great procession of the family goddess, and in that procession the new bride goes out to the temple of Girija, the goddess of the mountain."

She ended where she had begun, with the one thing that mattered more than any plan. "And if I do not obtain your grace, O lotus-eyed one, I will give up this body, worn thin by my vows. Even a hundred births would not change my choice."

The brahmana fell silent. Krishna had listened without moving, taking in the princess's love and her strategy as one single thing, as she had meant them to be. The message had found its home. What he said in answer, and the journey that followed, would belong to the night.
reflection: What is striking about Rukmini's message is that adoration and strategy are one and the same in it: she offers herself to Krishna and then, in the same breath, tells him exactly how to come and claim her. Even her fear — that Shishupala, like a jackal, would seize the lion's share — is expressed as devotion.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana also tells the story of Rukmini's marriage; the message as rendered here follows the Bhagavata Purana.
next_story_tease: Krishna heard the message out in silence, and before the night was over he was on the road to Vidarbha.
hero_scene: Krishna seated in the lamplit hall of Dwaraka, listening without moving as the brahmana delivers Rukmini's words, her message hanging in the quiet air between them.
